extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, writers, and fans seeking an overview of mystery/detective fiction and its subgenres
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of genre conventions, subgenre distinctions, and historical/contextual features relevant to creating or analyzing mystery and detective fiction. Useful for writers, critics, and readers who need to know what elements define different kinds of mystery stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre definition: central mysterious event and resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery is a fiction genre where the nature of an event, often a murder or other crime, remains mysterious until the end of the story. Often within a closed circle of suspects, each suspect is usually provided with a credible motive and a reasonable opportunity for committing the crime. The central character is often a detective ... who eventually solves the mystery by logical deduction from facts presented to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle of fair presentation: the solution should follow from facts presented to the reader. Examples cited include Sherlock Holmes. Note that some books labelled 'mystery' may be non-fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis: puzzle/suspense and logical solution (vs. hardboiled action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery fiction can be detective stories in which the emphasis is on the puzzle or suspense element and its logical solution such as a whodunit. Mystery fiction can be contrasted with hardboiled detective stories, which focus on action and gritty realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing/assessing a mystery, determine whether the work privileges an intellectual puzzle and logical unraveling (classical mystery/whodunit) or prioritizes atmosphere, action, and realism (hardboiled).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed circle of suspects with motive and opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Often within a closed circle of suspects, each suspect is usually provided with a credible motive and a reasonable opportunity for committing the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A closed community setting (house, village, limited cast) helps create a solvable puzzle; suspects should be plausibly capable of committing the crime so the reader can weigh alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of clues, red herrings, plot twists, and detective denouement
rubrics_metrics.description: The detective story ... has clues, red herrings, some plot twists along the way and a detective denouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of deliberate red herrings and well-placed clues is a defining structural technique. The denouement should explain how the detective reached the solution and reconcile the clues and misdirections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair-play / reader-solve opportunity (whodunit principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whodunit is classified as a detective story where the reader is given clues throughout as to who the culprit is, giving the reader the opportunity to solve the crime before it is revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Golden Age convention: provide sufficient and not-contradicted evidence so attentive readers can deduce the culprit. Historically common in 1920s–1940s works and many female authors' whodunits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detective story vs mystery fiction: protagonist and focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The detective story shares some similarities with mystery fiction ... but differs on several points. Most Sherlock Holmes stories feature no suspects at all, while mystery fiction, in contrast, features a large number of them. Detective stories feature professional and retired detectives, while mystery fiction almost exclusively features amateur detectives. Finally, detective stories focus on the detective and how the crime was solved, while mystery fiction concentrates on the identity of the culprit and how the crime was committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or crafting a piece, note whether the narrative centers on the detective's methods/personality (detective story) or on the puzzle of 'who' and 'how' (mystery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cozy mystery conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cozy mysteries ... generally shy away from violence and suspense and frequently feature female amateur detectives. This genre features minimal violence, sex and social relevance, a solution achieved by intellect or intuition rather than police procedure, with order restored in the end, honorable characters, and a setting in a closed community. The murders are often committed by less violent tools such as poison and the wounds inflicted are rarely if ever used as clues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cozy rules: limit graphic content, emphasize intellect/intuition, use a contained community, restore social order, and avoid using injuries as forensic puzzle elements. Not strictly mandatory but typical expectations for readers/publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police procedural realism and institutional constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Police procedural stories try to realistically depict the routine activities of a group of police officers who are frequently working on more than one case simultaneously, providing a stark contrast to the detective-as-superhero archetype ... the police detective was subject to error and was constrained by rules and regulations. The detective in the police procedural does the things police officers do to catch a criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize realistic procedure, bureaucracy, fallibility, and multiple caseloads; accuracy in police work and institutional detail is a mark of the subgenre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Howcatchem / inverted detective story structure
rubrics_metrics.description: An inverted detective story, also known as a 'howcatchem', is a plot structure ... in which the commission of the crime is shown or described at the beginning, usually including the identity of the perpetrator. The story then describes the detective's attempt to solve the mystery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dramatic tension comes from the investigation and method rather than discovery of the culprit; may include subsidiary puzzles (e.g., motive) to resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardboiled fiction characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled is described as a genre that 'usually deals with criminal activity in a modern urban environment, a world of disconnected signs and anonymous strangers.' ... Very often, no actual mystery even existed: the books simply revolved around justice being served to those who deserved harsh treatment, which was described in explicit detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect terse/unemotional narration, urban grit, violence and sex, social commentary, and emphasis on action rather than puzzle-solving. Works may prioritize realism and the underworld over fair-play clueing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locked-room mystery conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The locked-room mystery is a subgenre ... The crime—almost always murder—is committed in circumstances under which it was seemingly impossible for the perpetrator to commit the crime and/or evade detection ... Following other conventions of classic detective fiction, the reader is normally presented with the puzzle and all of the clues, and is encouraged to solve the mystery before the solution is revealed in a dramatic climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an apparently impossible situation, but ensure a logical (often ingenious) explanation exists and that clues necessary to that explanation are available to the reader; emphasis on intellectual trickery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal thriller / courtroom novel features
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal thriller or courtroom novel ... The system of justice itself is always a major part of these works ... The legal thriller usually starts its business with the court proceedings following the closure of an investigation, often resulting in a new angle on the investigation, so as to bring about a final outcome different from the one originally devised by the investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center the judicial system and court process as active elements; expect legal strategy, courtroom drama, and how trials change case outcomes. Accuracy of legal procedure strengthens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical mystery setting requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: These works are set in a time period considered historical from the author's perspective, and the central plot involves the solving of a mystery or crime (usually murder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical accuracy in period details and social norms is important; integrate era-appropriate investigative methods and constraints into the puzzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occult detective fiction conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Occult detective fiction centers around the investigation of supernatural phenomena in the absence of or in concert with criminal investigation. Supernatural elements typically occur in a world where magic is not diegetically usual, common, or expected; other stories ... utilize phenomena to misdirect the reader and investigator from a solution grounded in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether supernatural elements are genuine or misdirection; balance investigative procedure with occult elements, and set reader expectations about plausibility within the story world.

rubrics_metrics.name: True crime characteristics (nonfiction distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: True crime is a literary genre that recounts real crimes committed by real people ... Unlike fiction of the kind, it does not focus much on the identity of the culprit and has no red herrings or clues, but often emphasizes how the culprit was caught and their motivations behind their actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating true crime, expect factual recounting, focus on capture and motive, ethical considerations regarding sensitivity to victims, and less emphasis on puzzle mechanics or reader-solve opportunity.
